reading.title: Choosing a drawing or model
reading.text: At a design review, Dina compares a blueprint with a floor plan. The floor plan shows rooms from above; an elevation shows a building face, and a cross-section shows a cut through it. A scale model is a reduced physical representation, while a rendering communicates the proposed appearance. Dina makes a sketch before opening CAD software. Her digital 3D model differs from the physical model on the desk. The site plan shows the building in its surroundings. At the drafting station, a T-square guides straight lines, a triangle provides fixed angles, and a compass draws circles. A protractor measures angles; a scale ruler helps interpret reduced dimensions. Dina checks what each representation shows before comparing the proposal's effects.

reading.title: Explaining visual relationships
reading.text: Dina prepares a draft on a drafting table. Tracing paper lets her compare an earlier layout with a new one. A pencil set offers different marks, and an eraser shield protects neighboring lines while she erases a small area. A French curve guides a smooth irregular curve. During the critique, proportion concerns relative sizes, while scale relates the representation to the actual building. Symmetry means corresponding parts across an axis; balance concerns the distribution of visual weight. Repeated elements create rhythm. Contrast distinguishes elements, unity makes them feel connected, and emphasis directs attention. Space concerns the arrangement of areas, whereas form concerns three-dimensional shape. Dina explains these relationships using the proposal, without treating a pleasing composition as proof of structural performance.

reading.title: Preparing a design presentation
reading.text: The studio prepares a client presentation. Dina uses a model making kit for a small physical mock-up. A laser cutter and 3D printer can produce different model components, but only trained staff operate them. A light table illuminates drawings from below. The pin-up board holds the drawings for the group discussion. Material samples let the client handle proposed finishes; color charts organize color choices. Reference books provide background information rather than decide the project. A projector displays an image for the room, while a plotter prints large drawings. Dina explains which choices are provisional and asks the team to reconcile design constraints. The presentation supports a discussion; it does not certify safety, compliance or the suitability of a material.
